title: Batch processing vs Stream processing: Spark batch for historical analysis, Flink/Kafka Streams for real-time.
keyPoints: Batch processing runs a job over a bounded dataset in one high-throughput pass; results are available only after the job completes.
Stream processing computes incrementally over an unbounded event flow with low latency as data arrives.
Spark is the dominant batch engine; Flink and Kafka Streams are common stream engines.
Use batch for historical analysis, end-of-day reports, reconciliation, and regulatory filings.
Use streaming for fraud detection, real-time dashboards, live alerts, and event-driven reactions.
Modern architectures run both: streaming for real-time reactions, batch for periodic authoritative recomputation.
Stream processing must handle event-time vs processing-time, watermarks for late data, and checkpointing for fault tolerance.

s1_definition.oneliner: Batch processes a bounded dataset in one high-throughput pass (Spark); streaming processes an unbounded event flow with low latency as it arrives (Flink/Kafka Streams).
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Batch processing** : runs a job over a large, bounded dataset collected over a period, optimized for throughput; Apache Spark is the dominant engine.
- **Stream processing** : computes results incrementally over an unbounded, continuous flow of events with low latency; Apache Flink and Kafka Streams are common engines.
- **Windowing** : grouping events by time intervals (tumbling, hopping, sliding) for stream aggregation.
- **Watermark** : a marker that tracks event-time progress so the system knows when a window can be finalized.
- **Checkpointing** : periodically saving stream state for fault-tolerant recovery without reprocessing everything.
s1_definition.analogy: At the end of each day, National Bank of India gathers every transaction and runs one big job to compute interest and reports : that is batch processing, done on a fixed pile of data overnight. But the fraud team needs to catch a suspicious transaction within seconds, so they watch the live stream and react immediately : that is stream processing. Batch is the overnight accountant; streaming is the real-time security guard.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Batch vs Stream Processing

  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                  Data Sources                    │
  │  Transactions, Events, Logs                      │
  └──────────────┬──────────────────┬────────────────┘
                 │                  │
         ┌───────▼───────┐  ┌──────▼────────┐
         │ Stream Path   │  │ Batch Path    │
         │ (Flink/KS)    │  │ (Spark)       │
         │               │  │               │
         │ Fraud detect  │  │ Interest calc │
         │ Live alerts   │  │ Reconciliation│
         │ RT dashboard  │  │ Reg. reports  │
         │               │  │               │
         │ Latency: secs │  │ Latency: hours│
         │ Continuous     │  │ Periodic      │
         └───────┬───────┘  └──────┬────────┘
                 │                  │
         ┌───────▼───────┐  ┌──────▼────────┐
         │ Real-time     │  │ Data warehouse│
         │ alerts topic  │  │ / reports     │
         └───────────────┘  └───────────────┘

  Stream windowing:
  Tumbling:  |──5min──|──5min──|──5min──|  (non-overlapping)
  Hopping:   |──5min──|
                |──5min──|
                   |──5min──|                (overlapping)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Batch and stream processing are two paradigms for computing over data, and I choose by latency need and data boundedness. Batch processing runs a job over a bounded dataset in one high-throughput pass, optimized for throughput, with results available only after completion. Spark is the dominant engine, and in banking I use batch for end-of-day interest, regulatory reports, and reconciliation.

Stream processing computes incrementally over an unbounded flow with low latency as each event arrives. Flink and Kafka Streams are the common engines. In banking I use streaming for fraud detection, real-time dashboards, and live alerts, where reacting within seconds is the entire value.

The two are complements, not competitors. Modern architectures run both: the streaming path handles real-time reactions while the batch path handles periodic, authoritative recomputation. At National Bank of India, a fraud alert fires in seconds on the stream, while overnight a Spark batch job recomputes complete interest totals and reconciles.

The senior insight is that batch is increasingly understood as a special case of streaming over a bounded source. The key decision is matching each workload to the right path rather than choosing one paradigm exclusively.

Remember one sentence: use streaming for low-latency reactions like fraud detection and batch for high-throughput historical analysis like interest calculation, and run both together in a unified architecture.
